title: CAP Theorem

options.a: A distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most two out of three guarantees: Consistency (linearizability), Availability, and Partition tolerance.
options.b: In a network partition, a distributed system can maintain both synchronous ACID transactions and infinite horizontal scalability.
options.c: Any distributed service with high partition tolerance automatically provides continuous read availability at the expense of storage durability.
options.d: Network latency can be traded for computational throughput as long as node partitions are resolved using two-phase locking.

title: PACELC Theorem

options.a: Posits that parallel asynchronous computing eliminates latency completely when caching nodes are collocated with client endpoints.
options.b: Extends CAP: if there is a Partition (P), trade Availability (A) vs Consistency (C); Else (E), trade Latency (L) vs Consistency (C).
options.c: States that partitioned architectures must enforce linear consistency before event-driven microservices emit asynchronous domain events.
options.d: Guarantees that asynchronous cluster topologies yield zero read latency whenever data is replicated across at least three cloud regions.

title: Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

options.a: An optimistic lock acquisition protocol where clients submit two version hashes before committing updates to a relational database.
options.b: A replication protocol that sends writes to both leader and standby replicas simultaneously before persisting to disk.
options.c: An atomic commitment protocol where a coordinator polls participants in a Prepare phase, then issues a global Commit or Rollback in a Commit phase.
options.d: An asynchronous batching technique that aggregates microservice transactions into dual persistent log buffers.

title: Saga Pattern

options.a: Replaces relational database tables with decentralized append-only event logs to ensure zero read latency across service boundaries.
options.b: Guarantees immediate ACID consistency across multiple microservices by utilizing a shared distributed lock manager.
options.c: A caching strategy that writes cache entries to intermediate memory before flushing dirty buffers to downstream storage.
options.d: Manages distributed transactions across microservices as a sequence of local transactions, executing compensating transactions on failure.

title: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)

options.a: Separates read and write data models, allowing reads and writes to scale, optimize, and evolve independently.
options.b: Enforces that all database mutations and queries must execute synchronously through a single consolidated SQL schema.
options.c: A network routing pattern where API commands bypass intermediate proxies while read queries traverse a caching reverse proxy.
options.d: A concurrency model where write locks prevent read transactions from accessing materialized cache views.

title: Event Sourcing

options.a: Replaces microservice REST endpoints with raw pub/sub brokers to broadcast HTTP request bodies directly to client browsers.
options.b: Persists the state of a business entity as an immutable, append-only sequence of state-changing domain events rather than mutating current values.
options.c: A database indexing technique that pre-computes aggregate values whenever a transaction commits to the write-ahead log.
options.d: An asynchronous logging framework that streams server error logs to a centralized elasticsearch observability cluster.

title: Idempotency & Idempotency Key

options.a: A hashing mechanism that guarantees cryptographic uniqueness for user passwords before storing them in database tables.
options.b: A database constraint that prevents concurrent transactions from modifying adjacent table partitions during schema migrations.
options.c: The property where an operation can be applied multiple times without changing the result beyond the initial application, often tracked via a unique request token.
options.d: A network retry algorithm that exponentially reduces backoff intervals when upstream gateway connections fail.

title: Backpressure

options.a: The pressure exerted on network switches when TCP packet windows exceed the physical throughput of fiber cables.
options.b: A database lock escalation strategy that pauses low-priority reads when write transaction buffers are exhausted.
options.c: An observability alerting threshold triggered when upstream API gateway error rates exceed 5% over a 5-minute rolling window.
options.d: A feedback mechanism where a downstream consumer signals an upstream producer to slow down or halt data transmission when overwhelmed.

title: Circuit Breaker Pattern

options.a: Prevents an application from repeatedly attempting an operation likely to fail, transitioning between Closed, Open, and Half-Open states to protect downstream services.
options.b: An electrical safety device configured in cloud data centers to isolate rack servers drawing excess electrical current.
options.c: A network routing rule that drops inbound HTTP requests if the client IP appears in an automated abuse blacklist.
options.d: A concurrency primitive that terminates background worker threads when aggregate CPU utilization crosses 90%.

title: Bulkhead Pattern

options.a: Replaces synchronous HTTP REST communication with asynchronous AMQP messaging queues across all core services.
options.b: Isolates elements of an application into distinct pools (threads, connections, resources) so that if one fails, the others continue functioning.
options.c: Encrypts inter-service network packets using ephemeral session keys to prevent lateral movement after a perimeter breach.
options.d: A blue-green deployment strategy where user traffic is duplicated across two isolated container clusters simultaneously.

title: Transactional Outbox Pattern

options.a: Sends unread user notifications to an external dead-letter queue when SMS gateway webhooks return 500 status codes.
options.b: Caches outbound HTTP responses in an edge CDN layer to avoid re-executing business logic on repeated client requests.
options.c: Writes domain events to an outbox table in the same local database transaction as business entities, ensuring reliable at-least-once publishing to message brokers.
options.d: Automatically rolls back distributed database transactions if downstream subscribers fail to acknowledge messages within 30 seconds.

title: Change Data Capture (CDC)

options.a: Automatically compresses cold database tables into columnar Parquet files once rows exceed 90 days of age.
options.b: An HTTP header negotiation protocol that caches client request bodies before submitting them to payment gateways.
options.c: A schema migration tool that captures diffs between staging and production database DDL scripts.
options.d: A technique that monitors and captures row-level inserts, updates, and deletes from a database's transaction log in real time.

title: Consistent Hashing

options.a: A hashing scheme where resizing the node cluster remaps on average only K/N keys, minimizing cache misses during horizontal scaling.
options.b: A cryptographic hashing function that ensures deterministic password hashing across distributed CPU architectures.
options.c: A database sharding algorithm that requires complete re-indexing of all table rows whenever a new shard is provisioned.
options.d: A network checksum algorithm that detects packet corruption across fiber optic WAN connections.

title: Split-Brain Problem

options.a: When an individual engineer attempts to maintain two divergent feature branches concurrently without rebasing.
options.b: A distributed cluster condition where network partitioning isolates sub-clusters, each mistakenly believing it is the sole active authority and accepting conflicting writes.
options.c: A memory corruption bug in multi-threaded runtimes where two CPU cores overwrite the same pointer address.
options.d: When an API gateway routes identical user requests to two different versions of a microservice simultaneously.

title: Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT)

options.a: A fault-tolerance mechanism designed exclusively to prevent hardware memory bit-flips in cosmic-ray exposed satellites.
options.b: A protocol that guarantees distributed transactions complete even when network latency reaches tens of seconds.
options.c: The ability of a distributed network to reach consensus even when components fail arbitrarily or transmit conflicting/malicious information.
options.d: An architectural rule requiring microservices to implement automatic fallback responses when third-party vendors fail.

title: SLA vs SLO vs SLI

options.a: SLA, SLO, and SLI are interchangeable terms describing network packet loss thresholds across API load balancers.
options.b: SLA is an internal team guideline, SLO is a customer contract, and SLI is the automated deployment pipeline health check.
options.c: SLI measures system revenue, SLO measures cloud infrastructure expenses, and SLA measures developer sprint velocity.
options.d: SLI is the quantified metric (e.g. latency), SLO is the internal target (e.g. 99.9%), and SLA is the business contract with penalties.

title: Error Budget

options.a: The permitted level of unreliability (1 - SLO) that a service can incur before feature releases are halted in favor of reliability work.
options.b: The maximum financial expense allocated by leadership for third-party bug bounty vulnerability programs.
options.c: A strict database transaction quota that limits how many failed queries a single tenant can submit per hour.
options.d: The total number of compilation and linter errors permitted on pull requests before CI branch protection triggers.

title: Four Golden Signals

options.a: CPU, Memory, Disk I/O, and Network Bandwidth consumption tracked across bare-metal server nodes.
options.b: Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation, as defined in Google's Site Reliability Engineering framework.
options.c: Unit test coverage, integration pass rate, build duration, and pull request review turnaround time.
options.d: Throughput, Cache Hit Ratio, Thread Pool Exhaustion, and Garbage Collection pause frequency.

title: RED Method

options.a: A frontend performance rubric tracking Rendering speed, Execution pauses, and DOM size.
options.b: A server hardware troubleshooting technique monitoring RAID disks, Ethernet cards, and Dual-in-line memory modules.
options.c: A microservices monitoring philosophy focusing on Rate (requests/sec), Errors (failed requests), and Duration (latency).
options.d: A cloud disaster recovery framework prioritizing Regional failover, Edge DNS routing, and Database replication.

title: USE Method

options.a: A security auditing protocol auditing User permissions, Session cookies, and Endpoint authorization headers.
options.b: A database schema optimization strategy indexing Unique constraints, Surrogate keys, and Entity relationships.
options.c: A software estimation heuristic evaluating User stories, Story points, and Estimated release sprints.
options.d: A system performance methodology (Brendan Gregg) analyzing every resource for Utilization, Saturation, and Errors.

title: MTTR vs MTTD vs MTBF

options.a: MTTD is Mean Time To Detect, MTTR is Mean Time To Recovery/Repair, and MTBF is Mean Time Between Failures.
options.b: MTTR is Mean Time To Reboot, MTTD is Mean Time To Deploy, and MTBF is Mean Time Before Financial loss.
options.c: MTTD measures testing duration, MTTR measures code review time, and MTBF measures branch checkout frequency.
options.d: MTTR, MTTD, and MTBF are cryptographic key rotation metrics enforced in SOC2 Type II compliance audits.

title: Thundering Herd Problem

options.a: When multiple background cron jobs execute database migrations on the primary database simultaneously.
options.b: When thousands of concurrent requests all miss a cache simultaneously and slam the upstream database/backend at once.
options.c: A memory allocation spike caused when Node.js runs garbage collection on multiple worker threads at once.
options.d: When all distributed cluster nodes attempt to write to the same Kafka partition simultaneously.

title: Cascading Failure

options.a: When CSS style rules conflict across child DOM elements, creating unresponsive layout reflows.
options.b: An automated testing failure where one broken unit test causes subsequent integration suites to abort.
options.c: A failure in one component that increases load or triggers faults in neighboring components, dominoing across the entire system.
options.d: When database foreign keys cascade-delete child rows unexpectedly across relational tables.

title: OpenTelemetry: Spans, Traces, & Baggage

options.a: Spans and Traces are proprietary AWS CloudWatch features designed to measure serverless Lambda invocation billings.
options.b: Spans represent database table indexes, Traces represent network routing hops, and Baggage measures byte size of request headers.
options.c: A Trace is an error log dump, a Span is a CPU profile graph, and Baggage is the container image layer metadata.
options.d: A Trace represents a complete request journey through a distributed system, composed of individual Spans, while Baggage propagates contextual key-value pairs.

title: Blameless Post-Mortem

options.a: An incident review process assuming people made reasonable choices with the information they had, focusing on systemic fixes rather than punishment.
options.b: An incident review where legal counsel redacts all engineer identities before filing insurance claims.
options.c: An automated GitHub Action that closes incident tickets if no code changes caused the production outage.
options.d: A management meeting where the engineer responsible for a bug is reassigned to another engineering department.

title: Chaos Engineering

options.a: Deploying untested feature branches directly to production during peak holiday traffic without code reviews.
options.b: The discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in the system's capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production.
options.c: A software architecture methodology that eliminates all static typing in favor of dynamic runtime metaprogramming.
options.d: An agile sprint practice where engineers work on unassigned tickets without product manager oversight.

title: High Water Mark (HWM) & Low Water Mark (LWM)

options.a: Browser viewport scroll positions used in infinite scroll lists to load secondary DOM elements.
options.b: The highest and lowest historical stock valuations used to price engineering equity grants.
options.c: Threshold boundaries used in memory allocators, log replication, and cache eviction to trigger buffer flushes or mark committed offsets.
options.d: Cloud security metrics tracking maximum and minimum firewall intrusion attempts per day.

title: Load Shedding & Graceful Degradation

options.a: Shutting down the production database every Sunday morning to allow offline vacuuming and disk defragmentation.
options.b: Compressing old relational database records into zip archives to free up block storage capacity.
options.c: Offloading user password validation to third-party public DNS resolvers during traffic spikes.
options.d: Deliberately rejecting non-critical or excess requests to preserve capacity and prevent complete collapse of core functionality under extreme load.

title: Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)

options.a: A dedicated queue or storage destination where messages that cannot be processed successfully after maximum retries are isolated for analysis.
options.b: A temporary buffer in email servers where unsent promotional emails are discarded after 24 hours.
options.c: A database recycle bin where dropped SQL tables are stored before final disk deletion.
options.d: A network router buffer that discards malformed TCP packets before they reach application sockets.

title: Conway's Law

options.a: Software complexity doubles every eighteen months unless aggressive refactoring sprints are scheduled by engineering leadership.
options.b: Organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations.
options.c: Adding more developers to an overdue software project invariably makes the delivery date even later.
options.d: Every microservice will eventually grow until it requires its own dedicated relational database cluster.

title: Hyrum's Law

options.a: Any software system that can be rewritten in Rust will eventually be rewritten in Rust.
options.b: The time required to fix a software defect in production is inversely proportional to the clarity of the error logs.
options.c: With a sufficient number of users of an API, all observable behaviors of the system will be depended on by somebody, regardless of the contract.
options.d: Network latency between microservices increases linearly with every additional serialization boundary.

title: Chesterton's Fence

options.a: A network firewall principle requiring all outbound traffic to traverse a centralized corporate proxy.
options.b: A code review guideline stating that pull requests should touch no more than 200 lines of code.
options.c: A database partitioning technique where hot tables are quarantined behind read-only replicas.
options.d: Do not remove a fence, rule, or piece of legacy code until you understand the original reason why it was put there in the first place.

title: Gall's Law

options.a: A complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked. A complex system designed from scratch never works.
options.b: Software bugs cluster together in modules that have the highest number of cyclomatic branching conditions.
options.c: The amount of memory used by a program expands to fill the entire physical RAM available on the host machine.
options.d: System design documents longer than five pages have an exponential probability of remaining unread by the team.

title: Brooks' Law

options.a: Every software architecture eventually collapses under the weight of accumulated technical debt.
options.b: Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later, due to communication overhead and onboarding time.
options.c: The difficulty of refactoring legacy code increases with the square of the lines of code in the repository.
options.d: Developers spend 80% of their time reading code and only 20% of their time writing new code.

title: Law of Demeter (Principle of Least Knowledge)

options.a: Microservices should never expose their internal database connection strings across environment variables.
options.b: Engineers should only be granted read-only database credentials during active production investigations.
options.c: A software component should only speak to its immediate friends and avoid reaching through objects to talk to strangers (e.g. avoid a.getB().getC().doD()).
options.d: Client browsers should cache REST responses for no longer than sixty seconds to prevent stale data display.

title: Postel's Law (Robustness Principle)

options.a: API endpoints must deprecate legacy endpoints within 90 days of releasing a major version.
options.b: Software should reject any network packet that fails cryptographic checksum validation without inspection.
options.c: Relational database tables should enforce strict foreign key constraints across all transactional tables.
options.d: Be conservative in what you send, and liberal in what you accept (e.g. generate clean outputs, tolerate imperfect inputs).

title: SOLID: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

options.a: A class or module should have one, and only one, reason to change (gather together things that change for the same reason).
options.b: A microservice should execute exactly one HTTP request at a time to prevent multithreaded race conditions.
options.c: A software engineer should work on only one pull request at a time during an active sprint cycle.
options.d: A database table should contain exactly one primary key column and no foreign key references.

title: SOLID: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

options.a: Open source libraries should never be closed or re-licensed under commercial dual-licensing terms.
options.b: Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.
options.c: API connections must remain open during transactions but close immediately upon receiving 200 OK.
options.d: Classes should keep member fields open as public properties while keeping methods closed as private.

title: SOLID: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

options.a: Microservices in a cluster can be swapped with serverless cloud functions without altering client latency.
options.b: Relational database tables can be substituted with NoSQL document collections without changing business logic.
options.c: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program.
options.d: Synchronous HTTP endpoints should be substitutable with asynchronous WebSockets transparently.

title: SOLID: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

options.a: Database interfaces must be segregated from application business logic using an Object-Relational Mapper (ORM).
options.b: Public API gateways should enforce separate rate limiting tiers for mobile clients versus desktop clients.
options.c: Frontend user interfaces must be physically hosted on separate origin domains from backend API servers.
options.d: Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use (prefer small, role-specific interfaces).

title: SOLID: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

options.a: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details.
options.b: Package managers must resolve transitive library dependencies in reverse alphabetical order to avoid circular imports.
options.c: Frontend client applications should inject compiled CSS files at the end of the HTML document head.
options.d: Database migration scripts should depend on raw SQL statements rather than ORM entity classes.

title: DRY vs WET vs AHA

options.a: DRY, WET, and AHA are cloud cost optimization tiers for cold, warm, and archive object storage.
options.b: DRY is Don't Repeat Yourself, WET is Write Everything Twice, and AHA is Avoid Hasty Abstractions (favor duplication over the wrong abstraction).
options.c: DRY applies to database normalization, WET applies to frontend templating, and AHA applies to machine learning.
options.d: They are network compression algorithms used to compress HTTP response payloads across CDN edge nodes.

title: Strangler Fig Pattern

options.a: An anti-pattern where a slow microservice exhausts upstream thread pools until the entire cluster dies.
options.b: A software testing technique that aggressively truncates long-running test suites to speed up CI runs.
options.c: Gradually replacing a legacy system by incrementally replacing specific pieces of functionality with new services until the old system is retired.
options.d: A database compaction strategy that deletes obsolete table partitions during low-traffic overnight hours.

title: OAuth 2.0 vs OpenID Connect (OIDC)

options.a: OAuth 2.0 is designed exclusively for enterprise LDAP servers, while OIDC is designed for consumer mobile apps.
options.b: OAuth 2.0 and OIDC are competing incompatible standards for session cookie management.
options.c: OAuth 2.0 encrypts network payloads, while OIDC verifies client TLS certificates.
options.d: OAuth 2.0 provides authorization (delegated access via access tokens), while OIDC adds an identity and authentication layer (ID tokens).

title: JWT (JSON Web Token)

options.a: A compact, URL-safe means of representing claims between two parties, structured into three base64url parts: Header, Payload, and Signature.
options.b: A binary encryption algorithm used to hash passwords before storing them in relational database tables.
options.c: An HTTP header specification used to compress JSON payloads across high-latency cellular connections.
options.d: A proprietary session format used exclusively in Google Chrome browser extensions.

title: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange)

options.a: A public key encryption algorithm used to establish SSH connections to remote server terminals.
options.b: An extension to OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow that protects public clients (SPAs, mobile apps) against authorization code interception attacks.
options.c: A cryptographic database protocol used to encrypt table columns at rest using envelope encryption.
options.d: A mutual TLS authentication handshake executed between microservices inside a service mesh.

title: RBAC vs ABAC

options.a: RBAC encrypts symmetric keys, while ABAC encrypts asymmetric cryptographic key pairs.
options.b: RBAC is used for database indexing, while ABAC is used for message queue routing.
options.c: RBAC grants permissions based on static roles, whereas ABAC grants permissions dynamically based on attributes (user, resource, environment).
options.d: RBAC is an agile project management term, while ABAC is an SRE incident metric.

title: Mutual TLS (mTLS)

options.a: A web browser caching mechanism that stores SSL certificates in local storage.
options.b: A load balancing algorithm that duplicates TCP connection handshakes across dual network switches.
options.c: An encryption scheme where database backups are encrypted with two distinct private keys simultaneously.
options.d: A two-way authentication process where both the client and server authenticate each other using X.509 digital certificates.

title: Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA)

options.a: A security model based on the principle of 'never trust, always verify', requiring strict identity verification for every user and device, even inside the perimeter.
options.b: A software development culture where developers refuse to review pull requests submitted by other teams.
options.c: A testing framework that deletes all mock data from integration test suites to ensure real database execution.
options.d: A cloud architecture that eliminates external internet gateways by hosting services solely on local on-premise hardware.

title: Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP)

options.a: Limiting the number of software engineers permitted to submit pull requests on core repositories.
options.b: Giving a user, process, or system only the minimum necessary permissions required to perform its valid function, and nothing more.
options.c: Restricting microservice CPU utilization to less than 50% during non-peak business hours.
options.d: Ensuring database transactions acquire row-level locks rather than table-level locks.

title: Defense in Depth

options.a: Writing unit tests, integration tests, end-to-end tests, and performance benchmarks for every codebase module.
options.b: Deploying Kubernetes clusters across at least three geographic cloud regions simultaneously.
options.c: A cybersecurity strategy employing multiple layers of defensive controls throughout an information technology system to protect assets.
options.d: Stashing database write logs across multiple NVMe drives to prevent transaction data loss.

title: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)

options.a: An HTTP header that compresses image payloads when requested from mobile devices.
options.b: A server-to-server protocol used to replicate database records across different cloud availability zones.
options.c: A backend caching framework that distributes REST responses across multiple proxy servers.
options.d: A browser security mechanism allowing a server to declare which external origins are permitted to read its responses.

title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vs CSRF

options.a: XSS injects malicious client-side code into the victim's browser, while CSRF tricks an authenticated user's browser into executing unwanted actions.
options.b: XSS attacks database SQL servers, while CSRF attacks network domain name servers (DNS).
options.c: XSS targets backend microservice containers, while CSRF targets mobile push notification services.
options.d: XSS and CSRF are identical terms describing buffer overflow attacks in C++ runtimes.

title: Content Security Policy (CSP)

options.a: A legal privacy document required by the European Union under GDPR for user data processing.
options.b: An HTTP response header allowing site administrators to declare approved sources of content that browsers are permitted to load and execute.
options.c: A content delivery network caching policy controlling how edge nodes invalidate static image files.
options.d: A backend database constraint that restricts the character length of text columns in SQL schemas.

title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)

options.a: A network error where DNS servers return mismatched IP addresses for cloud load balancers.
options.b: A vulnerability where clients forge JWT token signatures using broken HMAC keys.
options.c: An attack where a threat actor abuses server functionality to force the backend server to make unauthorized requests to internal-only resources.
options.d: When client browsers submit forged CSRF tokens in order to bypass web application firewalls.

title: ReDoS (Regular Expression Denial of Service)

options.a: A database query planner bug where regex LIKE matches bypass table B-Tree indexes.
options.b: A brute-force network attack that saturates DNS servers with repeated regex pattern queries.
options.c: A memory leak caused by compiling regular expressions repeatedly inside tight JavaScript loops.
options.d: A denial-of-service attack caused by catastrophic backtracking in unoptimized regex patterns when evaluating malicious input.

title: ACID vs BASE

options.a: ACID is for relational databases (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability); BASE is for distributed stores (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency).
options.b: ACID refers to SQL syntax compilation, while BASE refers to NoSQL JSON document serialization formats.
options.c: ACID is a frontend state management framework, while BASE is a cloud object storage protocol.
options.d: ACID and BASE are identical database durability certifications governed by ISO/IEC standards.

title: OLTP vs OLAP vs HTAP

options.a: OLTP is used exclusively for machine learning pipelines, OLAP is for mobile apps, and HTAP is for edge CDNs.
options.b: OLTP is for fast row-oriented transactional processing, OLAP is for complex columnar analytical queries, and HTAP handles both concurrently.
options.c: OLTP, OLAP, and HTAP are database encryption algorithms used for sensitive financial data.
options.d: OLTP handles graph database queries, OLAP handles relational tables, and HTAP handles key-value caches.

title: Read-Your-Writes (Read-After-Write Consistency)

options.a: A caching rule where read operations are executed from disk while write operations are buffered in RAM.
options.b: A database constraint that prohibits users from reading table records until all active write locks are cleared.
options.c: A consistency guarantee ensuring that once a user updates a data item, any subsequent read by that same user will observe the updated value.
options.d: A transaction mode where write queries automatically echo back the modified row in the HTTP response body.

title: Isolation Levels: Dirty Read, Non-Repeatable Read, Phantom Read

options.a: Three network packet anomalies that occur when TCP connections drop packets during retransmission.
options.b: Three memory corruption errors in multi-core processors executing asynchronous memory barriers.
options.c: Three database disk errors that occur when write-ahead log files are corrupted during power loss.
options.d: Three concurrency phenomena: reading uncommitted data (Dirty), reading modified data mid-transaction (Non-Repeatable), and reading newly inserted rows (Phantom).

title: Write Skew

options.a: A race condition where concurrent transactions read overlapping state, make disjoint updates based on that state, and violate an application invariant.
options.b: An imbalance in distributed database shards where one node receives 90% of write traffic.
options.c: A physical disk sector degradation caused by repeatedly overwriting the same NAND flash block.
options.d: When database WAL logs are written out-of-order due to asynchronous Linux file system flushes.

title: Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)

options.a: A git branching strategy that manages concurrent releases across multiple open-source project versions.
options.b: A concurrency control method where database engines maintain multiple versions of data items so readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers.
options.c: A microservice deployment technique where multiple versions of an API run in production simultaneously.
options.d: A database schema versioning tool that records every ALTER TABLE statement in an audit table.

title: LSM-Tree vs B-Tree

options.a: B-Trees store data in flat text files, while LSM-Trees store data in memory-mapped binary trees.
options.b: B-Trees are used exclusively in graph databases, while LSM-Trees are used exclusively in relational databases.
options.c: B-Trees optimize for read throughput with in-place updates; LSM-Trees optimize for write throughput by writing to memory and sequentially appending to SSTables.
options.d: B-Trees and LSM-Trees are identical indexing structures with different patent licensing restrictions.

title: Write Amplification vs Read Amplification

options.a: Write Amplification is an agile metric measuring code churn, while Read Amplification measures code review comments.
options.b: Write Amplification measures network packet duplication, while Read Amplification measures CDN cache hit rates.
options.c: They measure the ratio of SQL queries generated by an Object-Relational Mapper relative to hand-written SQL.
options.d: Write Amplification is the ratio of bytes written to storage vs bytes requested; Read Amplification is the number of disk reads needed per logical read.

title: Bloom Filter

options.a: A space-efficient probabilistic data structure used to test whether an element is definitely not in a set or may be in a set.
options.b: A cryptographic hash function used to detect data tampering across distributed blockchain networks.
options.c: An image compression algorithm used to render blurred thumbnails during web page pre-loading.
options.d: A routing algorithm used in peer-to-peer networks to calculate shortest network paths between nodes.

title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Concurrency Control (OCC vs PCC)

options.a: OCC is used for batch processing jobs, while PCC is used for real-time video streaming.
options.b: PCC acquires locks upfront assuming conflicts will happen; OCC allows transactions to proceed without locks, validating for conflicts before commit.
options.c: PCC encrypts database columns before saving, while OCC encrypts records during network transmission.
options.d: OCC and PCC are competing CPU instruction set architectures used in ARM server processors.

title: Compare-And-Swap (CAS)

options.a: A database indexing strategy that swaps B-Tree leaf pages with hash map buckets during heavy query loads.
options.b: A cloud storage migration protocol that copies files between AWS S3 and Google Cloud Storage.
options.c: An atomic CPU instruction that compares the contents of a memory location with a given value and, only if they match, modifies the contents to a new given value.
options.d: A network protocol that swaps TCP SYN packets with UDP datagrams to bypass firewalls.

title: Starvation vs Deadlock vs Livelock

options.a: Starvation, Deadlock, and Livelock describe container scaling states in Kubernetes pod autoscalers.
options.b: Deadlock refers to disk failure, Livelock refers to memory exhaustion, and Starvation refers to CPU overheating.
options.c: They are three stages of database connection pool initialization in Apache Tomcat servers.
options.d: Deadlock: threads waiting on each other indefinitely; Livelock: threads active and changing state but making no progress; Starvation: a thread is perpetually denied resources.

title: DORA Metrics

options.a: Four key software delivery metrics: Deployment Frequency, Lead Time for Changes, Change Failure Rate, and Time to Restore Service.
options.b: Database operational metrics: Disk usage, Operation latency, Replication lag, and Availability percentage.
options.c: Frontend engineering benchmarks: DOM depth, Onload time, Render latency, and Asset bundle size.
options.d: Product management KPIs: Daily active users, Organic growth rate, Retention rate, and Average revenue per user.

title: Architecture Decision Record (ADR)
